summary_html: Reports via **state hotlines** (anonymous or confidential). CAPTA conditions funding on operating intake systems with confidentiality and good-faith protections.

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: B.H. v. County of San Bernardino
key_cases.holding: The court held that a law enforcement agency's CANRA duty to cross-report a child abuse report it receives to the county child welfare agency is a mandatory duty enforceable under Government Code section 815.6, distinct from the responding officer's separate investigative duties.
key_cases.relevance: Confirms that a hotline or 911 call received by a designated agency starts the statutory cross-reporting clock regardless of what the investigating officer later concludes.
key_cases.quote: These provisions indicate that a law enforcement agency's duty to cross-report the receipt of an initial child abuse or neglect report is separate from its investigative duties.

key_cases.holding: The court held that the absolute immunity Penal Code section 11172(a) confers on mandated reporters barred the parents' claims against the physician and hospital arising from a report of suspected child abuse, notwithstanding the loss of any civil remedy.
key_cases.relevance: Underpins the good-faith protection that makes anonymous and confidential hotline reporting workable in California.
key_cases.quote: The Legislature's solution in bestowing absolute immunity to the enumerated professionals was an attempt to remove one of the largest impediments to reporting
